issues.legal_issue: A grant to another holder does not transfer property already held under a separate grant unless the transfer is clearly shown.
material_facts: The village had been granted as a jagir to the respondent’s ancestors, and the appellants’ ancestor held it under a lease from a jagirdar.
The appellants relied on a later ruler’s bilmakta sanad and its schedule as including the village.
The village was listed under a heading identifying separate jagirs, and its revenue was excluded from the fixed amount of the bilmakta grant.
The sanad contained no clear indication that the earlier grant of the village had been taken away and transferred to the appellants’ ancestor.
issues.conclusion: The bilmakta sanad did not include the village, so the appellants acquired no right to it under that sanad.
issues.legal_principle: The scope of a grant must be determined from its terms and schedule. Where property was already granted to another holder, a later grant to someone else must clearly indicate that the earlier rights were taken away and the property was transferred. The court applied this principle to the sanad and its schedule; it also noted the absence of evidence that the earlier holder was informed of any such taking away.

rule.if: grant_scope_dispute_in_possession_suit and property_previously_held_under_separate_grant and grant_schedule_marks_property_as_separate and property_revenue_excluded_from_fixed_grant and not clear_transfer_of_prior_grant

predicates.grant_scope_dispute_in_possession_suit: The parties dispute in a possession suit whether a grant to one claimant included the property.
predicates.property_previously_held_under_separate_: The property was already held by another person under a separate grant.
predicates.grant_schedule_marks_property_as_separat: The schedule to the later grant identifies the property as separate from the property granted.
predicates.property_revenue_excluded_from_fixed_gra: The property’s revenue is excluded from the fixed amount stated in the later grant.
predicates.clear_transfer_of_prior_grant: The later grant clearly states that the earlier grant of the property was taken away and transferred.

issues.definition: When a possession suit concerns property already held under a separate grant, and the later grant marks it as separate, excludes its revenue, and does not clearly transfer the earlier grant, the later grant did not transfer the property.

issues.legal_issue: A lease that does not grant a permanent interest in its terms does not become a permanent lease merely because the lessee and successors remain in possession for a long time at the same rent.
material_facts: The lease granted the village for a fixed annual payment but specified no duration.
Its terms required annual payment in installments and did not state that the lease was permanent or that the payment could never be varied.
The appellants’ ancestor and successors remained in possession for more than a century at the same rent.
issues.conclusion: The lease did not grant a permanent lease, and the duration of possession at the same rent did not change its terms.
issues.legal_principle: The instrument must be read according to its plain terms; prolonged possession and payment of an unchanged rent do not make an otherwise non-permanent lease permanent. The court relied on the terms of the lease and rejected the claimed inference from long possession.

rule.if: lease_right_dispute_in_possession_suit and lease_sets_fixed_annual_payment and lease_specifies_no_duration and not lease_expressly_grants_permanent_interest and long_possession_at_same_rent

predicates.lease_right_dispute_in_possession_suit: The parties dispute in a possession suit whether a lease grants a permanent interest.
predicates.lease_sets_fixed_annual_payment: The lease requires payment of a fixed amount annually.
predicates.lease_specifies_no_duration: The lease states no duration for the grant.
predicates.lease_expressly_grants_permanent_interes: The lease expressly grants a permanent interest.
predicates.long_possession_at_same_rent: The lessee or successors remain in possession for a long period while paying the same rent.

issues.definition: In a possession suit, a lease setting a fixed annual payment but no duration or express permanent interest is not made permanent by long possession at the same rent.

issues.legal_issue: Adverse possession cannot establish a permanent lease against successive life-tenure jagirdars by combining time running against different holders when the original jagirdar lacked authority to grant beyond his lifetime.
material_facts: The property was held as a jagir, which was presumptively granted for the grantee’s lifetime unless the grant showed otherwise.
The jagir passed to successive holders as fresh grants, rather than as an inheritable estate held continuously under one title.
The lease was granted by a jagirdar who was not shown to have authority under the grant or state law to create a lease lasting beyond his lifetime.
The appellants relied on possession and an assertion of permanent lease rights dating from an earlier jagirdar’s tenure.
The suit was brought within the limitation period measured from the respondent’s acquisition of title as the current jagirdar.
issues.conclusion: The appellants did not acquire a permanent lease by adverse possession, and the suit was not barred by limitation.
issues.legal_principle: A limited interest can generally be acquired by adverse possession, as recognized in Sankaran v. Periasami, Thakore Fatehsingji Dipsangji v. Bamanji Ardeshir Dalal, and Shrimat Daivasikhamani Ponnambala Desikar v. Periayanan Chetti. But a jagir is prima facie for the grantee’s life (Gulabdas Jugjivandas v. The Collector of Surat); a family’s succession to a jagir does not make it permanent and hereditary where the State retains a right of resumption (Raje Vinaykrao Nemiwant Brahmin v. Raje Shriniwasrao Nemiwant Brahmin; Ahmad-un-Nissa Begum v. State). Each fresh grantee’s limitation period begins when that holder’s title accrues (Jagdish Narayan v. Nawab Saeed Ahmed Khan), and a jagirdar cannot grant a lease beyond his lifetime without authority under the grant or state law. The court distinguished Shrimat Daivasikhamani Ponnambala Desikar because a temple manager’s unauthorized lease could be voidable, whereas a jagirdar’s purported permanent lease was inoperative after his death and could be ignored by the succeeding grantee. Article 144 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, therefore did not allow time against one jagirdar to be tacked to time against another.

rule.if: adverse_possession_claim_in_possession_suit and jagir_is_life_tenure and each_successor_takes_fresh_grant and not jagirdar_authorized_to_grant_beyond_lifetime and suit_within_limitation_period_from_current_title

predicates.adverse_possession_claim_in_possession_s: A claimant in a possession suit asserts that adverse possession established a permanent lease or other limited interest.
predicates.jagir_is_life_tenure: The property is held under a grant that presumptively lasts only for the holder’s lifetime.
predicates.each_successor_takes_fresh_grant: A successor receives the property under a fresh grant rather than through continuous hereditary title.
predicates.jagirdar_authorized_to_grant_beyond_life: The grant or governing law authorizes the jagirdar to create a lease extending beyond the jagirdar’s lifetime.
predicates.suit_within_limitation_period_from_curre: The possession suit is brought before the limitation period has elapsed from the current holder’s acquisition of title.

issues.definition: Where a claimant asserts adverse possession of a permanent lease against successive life-tenure holders, each taking a fresh grant, and the original holder lacked authority to grant beyond life, the claimant acquires no permanent lease and a suit brought within the period measured from the current holder’s title is not time-barred.
